name: Assyrian ox gall hair dye

lead:
Clay tablets from the 7th century BCE are described as recording a hair dye made from ox gall, cypress oil, licorice and honey, used to turn grey hair black. It belongs to a long tradition of covering grey for a more youthful look, alongside Egyptian recipes for dyeing hair and eyebrows.
No laboratory or clinical studies have tested the recipe. It is known as a historical curiosity, and some modern readers treat it as an early natural-dye precedent.

paras: Historical sources describe a mixture of the four ingredients applied to grey hair to darken it. No reliable preparation details, quantities or durations are recorded.

No safety data exist for the recipe. Ox gall is a biological bile product, and anyone considering unfamiliar substances on skin or scalp is generally advised by dermatologists to consider allergy and irritation risks.

lead: The Assyrian ox gall hair dye is an ancient cosmetic recipe. According to Wikipedia's account of hair colouring, clay tablets from the 7th century BCE describe using ox gall, cypress oil, licorice and honey to turn grey hair black [1].

The point of such recipes was appearance: darkening grey hair to look younger or more polished. The same article notes that Assyrian herbals dated to around 2177 BCE are cited as holding some of the oldest known cosmetic recipes, and that the Egyptian Ebers Papyrus (c. 1550 BCE) includes recipes for dyeing grey hair and eyebrows [1].
No modern studies have tested the mixture. It is of interest mostly as part of the history of hair dye.

paras: The recipe as summarised in modern histories combines four ingredients: ox gall, cypress oil, licorice and honey. It is recorded for turning grey hair black [1].

Hair dyeing is described as an ancient art. Assyrian herbal texts, with a date of about 2177 BCE given in one account, are cited as containing some of the oldest known cosmetic recipes, and 7th century BCE clay tablets describe the ox gall mixture [1]. Egyptian sources such as the Ebers Papyrus (c. 1550 BCE) include recipes for dyeing grey hair and eyebrows, and the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus described Celts lightening their hair with lime [1].
Other ancient dyes were plant-based, for example henna, indigo, senna and black walnut hulls [1].
